titleStmt.title: Extract from Protocol No. 12, of the session of 26 June, 1880.

div.head: Extract from Protocol No. 12, of the session of 26 June, 1880.
div.p: Present, the ministers plenipotentiary of Germany, Austria-Hungary, Belgium, Spain, the United States of America, France, Great Britain, Denmark, Italy, Morocco, The Netherlands, Portugal, and Sweden and Norway.
The session opens at one o’clock.

The president observes that the conference, having accomplished its task even beyond its expectations, is on the eve of adjournment. He must, however, bring to the knowledge of its members, before they separate, an important communication addressed by the Holy See to the Government of His Catholic Majesty.

Mr. Cánovas del Castillo reads the following translation of a letter dated 4th of May, 1880, which he has received from His Eminence Cardinal Nina:
“Excellency: The Holy Father, obedient to the duties of his apostolic mission, cannot but profit by all the occasions which may offer to watch over the interests of Catholicism in whatever region of the globe. Having learned that, in the course of this month, a diplomatic congress is to be assembled under your presidency to treat of the affairs of Morocco, His Holiness, while recognizing the fact that among the questions to be submitted to the deliberations of the conference that touching religious liberty in the Moorish Empire has not been especially designated, believes, however, that nothing would prevent the plenipotentiaries assembled at Madrid from giving their attention to a subject so important to the welfare of the inhabitants of Morocco, even if only considered from the practical point of view.
“It is not to be’ doubted that, even as in the late congress of Berlin, the appeal made by my illustrious predecessor, Cardinal Franchi, to the representatives of France and Austria, Messrs. Waddington and Andrássy, resulted in the consideration and adoption, with general approval, of the demands of His Holiness relative to the freedom of the Catholic religion to the subjects of the Sublime Porte and of the neighboring
states, so likewise now the proposition which I make will be no less favorably received on the part of the worthy representatives who are about to meet in the capital of a nation so devoted to the Holy See and bound by so many interests to the Empire of Morocco. On the other hand, it is not allowable to suppose that the Moorish Government, bound by so strong a tie to the Supreme Representative of Islamism, can refuse to follow the example afforded by the adhesion of the Emperor of the Ottomans to the articles stipulated in the congress of Berlin, when the conference now about to meet shall propose to him the adoption of a similar resolution.
“Obeying these considerations, the Holy Father has charged me to address your excellency, the worthy presiding officer of this assemblage, and to appeal, in his pontifical name, to your sentiments as a Catholic and as a Spaniard to the end that he may be pleased to take charge of proposing and maintaining before the congress the proposition I have indicated, to the effect that the subjects of the Sultan, as well as foreigners, shall enjoy in Morocco the free exercise of the Catholic worship without thereby suffering wrong or prejudice in their civil or political rights.
“The Holy Father is not unaware of the obstacles which the present state of Morocco offers to the realization of this freedom; but these obstacles, far from discouraging, should stimulate all generous hearts who regard only the greatness of the end to be attained.
“For the rest, this principle once accepted and an engagement entered into with the foreign powers to conform therewith, if these powers, in unison with Spain, whose relations with Morocco are of a special character, should wish to take a ground similar to that adopted by them in the East, it could reasonably be hoped that the progress of civilization would soon bring about, by peaceful means, the free exercise of the Catholic worship in these African regions.
“In conformity with the orders of the august Pontiff, I must at the same time inform you that the Holy Father is animated by the intimate conviction that you will respond to his paternal appeal, and that the representatives of the other powers will second your efforts by receiving with favor a request in consonance with the received modern principles of public international law.
“The Holy Father likewise believes that by thus acting your excellency will respond to the well-known sentiments of His Majesty the King, your august sovereign, in favor of our holy religion.
“I earnestly avail myself of this occasion, &c.,
“L. Cardinal NINA.
“To his excellency Mr. Cánovas del Castillo.”

Mr. Cánovas del Castillo has had the honor to answer Monsignore, the apostolic nuncio at Madrid, with whom he has conferred on this subject, that the plenipotentiary of Spain was ready to present, and support, in the conference, the proposition of the Holy See, so soon as he could be assured that the representatives of the other powers would consent to consider questions outside of those which formed the object of their meeting; he should, in particular, consult his colleague, the representative of Great Britain, whose government had taken the initiative in calling the plenipotentiaries together, as to the opportuneness of bringing this proposition before the conference. Mr. Cánovas added that, if the conference should admit, in principle, the possibility of treating of questions foreign to the precise end proposed for it, the plenipotentiary of Spain would have the honor to fulfill the mission which the Holy See had deigned to confide to him, and that he felt persuaded that the communication from the Holy Father would, in this event, be received with all the deference due to its high orign.

He recalled at the same time the fact that the treaty of 1861 assures religious liberty to Spanish Catholics in Morocco, and that, moreover, the English treaty of 1856 likewise stipulated for British subjects the free exercise of their worship.

Having subsequently become convinced that the plenipotentiaries are disposed to examine this question, the president thinks that the conference ought to make a declaration, erecting into a general rule the principle which Morocco has already admitted by her treaties.

The Austro-Hungarian plenipotentiary, speaking next, says that the government of His Imperial and Royal Apostolic Majesty, in consequence of a similar overture on the part of the Holy See, has for his part assured himself that the other cabinets would be, in fact, .disposed to join in a declaration like that toward which the president of the conference had taken the initiative, provided that this declaration should be expressed in favor of all the non-Mussulman inhabitants of Morocco, and that the conference should at the same time recommend to the wisdom of the Sultan of Morocco the abolition of the disabilities which still weigh upon certain classes of his subjects by reason of their religious belief. It is in this sense, therefore, and in order to give a more precise form to this declaration, that Count Ludolf has been charged with the preparation of the draft of an address to the sovereign of Morocco, which he has the honor to submit to the conference.

The plenipotentiary of Austria-Hungary thereupon reads the document in these terms:
“On the eve of its dissolution, the conference, being informed by its president of the demand put forth on behalf of the Catholic Church by His Holiness the Sovereign Pontiff, in the letter which has just been read, asks, in its turn, that the free exercise of all worships be recognized in Morocco.
“The conference is the more convinced that this wish will be favorably received by His Sheriffian Majesty, inasmuch as the illustrious sovereign of Morocco has already given evident proof of his tolerance and his solicitude for the welfare of his non-Mussulman subjects by confirming, in 1874, the decree accorded by His Majesty the Sultan Sidi Mohammed, under date of 26th Chaban, 1280 (February, 1864), to Sir Moses Montefiore, which decree proclaims that all the subjects of the Moorish Empire shall have the same rank before the law; whence it follows that the Jews in Morocco should be treated conformably to justice and equity, and that no violence is to be shown with respect to either their persons or their property.
“As the result of this decree, many humiliating edicts and laws against non-Musselmans in former times have become obsolete, and the lot of the non-Mussulman races in Morocco has become more endurable.
“Nevertheless, these laws are not yet all formally revoked, and some of them even continue in force in more than one locality in the interior of the empire. Thus, the free exercise of their religion is not yet accorded in a legal manner to the non-Mussulman subjects of His Sheriffian Majesty, and many restrictions still exist for them, which are contrary to the spirit of the decree of 26 Chaban, 1280, and to the rule, at once so elemental and so universally respected, that the subjects of one and the same country, of whatever race or religion they may be, when faithfully fulfilling their duties toward the sovereign, should enjoy perfect identity of rights and complete equality before the law.
“Sultan Abd-ul Medjid, Emperor of the Ottomans, so long ago as 1839, by the hattisherif of Gulhané, spontaneously recognized and embodied in the legislation of his country this same principle, which has since been developed and confirmed by his successors, once in 1856 and latterly again in 1878, so that there can be no doubt that it is perfectly in accord with the Mohammedan law.
“Although persuaded that the illustrious sovereign of Morocco is animated, no less than the Sultan of Turkey, by benevolent intentions toward his non-Mussulman subjects, the conference would regard it as falling short of its duty did it not testify to the lively and profound interest it takes in the prompt amelioration of their lot. With this aim, the conference, in the name of the high powers represented therein, makes an appeal to His Sheriffian Majesty to the end that he, being faithful to his sentiments of justice and generosity, shall manifest that it is his firm determination—
“1st. To cause to be respected in his states the principle that all those now dwelling and who shall hereafter dwell therein shall profess and exercise without hinderance their modes of worship.
“2d. To prescribe to his government, as the immutable base of the legislation of Morocco, the maxim already adopted in the decree of 26th Chaban, 1280, according to which neither religion nor race can ever be the motive for setting up a difference in the manner of treatment, by and before the law, between his Mussulman and non-Mussulman subjects, neither can they serve as a pretext for imposing humiliations upon the latter, for depriving them of any civil right whatever, or for preventing them from exercising freely all the professions and industries which are permitted to the Mussulman subjects of the empire.
“Such a manifestation would not only honor the reign of His Sheriffian Majesty, but would likewise inaugurate for his states a new era of prosperity.
“The undersigned, in placing the present act in the hands of his excellency Sid Mohammed Vargas, beg that the minister plenipotentiary of Morocco will transmit it to His Sheriffian Majesty, who certainly will not refuse to it the serious attention which is due to a desire expressed in the name of the powers which the undersigned have the honor to represent.
“Madrid, June 26, 1880.”

This text is approved by the plenipotentiaries, with the exception of the representative of His Sheriffian Majesty, who can merely engage to bring to the cognizance of his sovereign the desires which the plenipotentiaries have thus expressed in the name of their respective governments.

Sid Mohammed Vargas, however, deems it due that he should recall to mind that in Morocco the Mussulmans, the Christians, and the Jews follow their religions without any hinderance or obstacle being set in the way thereof. The plenipotentiary of Morocco has no instructions from his sovereign which permit him to discuss this question, or any other which, like this, is not directly related to the object of his mission to Madrid. Nevertheless, in view of the address which the conference has just agreed upon, he deems it due to communicate thereto a letter which he has received from His Majesty the Sultan Muley el Hassan, and which concerns his Jewish subjects. He thereupon reads it in these terms:
“Praise to the One God! May the blessing of God be upon Mohammed, our lord and master, upon his family, and upon his comrades!
“To our esteemed servant, the Taleb Mohammed Vargas, may God prosper thee, and may peace be upon thee and likewise the benediction of the Most High God and His Mercy!
“And then:
“It has come to our knowledge that certain Jews among our subjects have made complaint again and again to their brethren dwelling in Europe, and to the foreign representatives at Tangier, that they cannot obtain justice for their complaints touching murders, robberies, and the like. They pretend that the governors show great indifference in procuring for them satisfaction from the persons who attack them, and that their grievances never reach our Sheriffian Majesty except through the medium of those persons (the Jews residing in Europe and the foreign representatives).
“Our Sheriffian will is that they shall obtain justice without the intercession of the powers or of the representatives, because they are our subjects and pay tribute unto us, having thereby the same rights as Mussulmans before us, and all abuses against them being forbidden by our religion.
“Wherefore, we command thee to hear the grievance of every Jew who may complain of not obtaining justice from a governor, and to lay it before us, whenever thou shalt find not the means of setting it right.
“We have sent orders in this wise to the governors of the cities, of the ports, and in the open country, to the end that they shall give knowledge thereof to the Jews, and at the same time we have warned them that if any one among them raises obstacles or prevents the complaint of a Jew coming even unto thee, we will punish him very sorely.
“We command thee to treat their business with all justice, and to hide from us nothing touching the doings of the governors toward them, for all men are equal before us in the matter of justice.
“22 Joumadi first, 1297.”

The President, in acknowledging this communication formally to the representative of Morocco, declares, in the name of all the plenipotentiaries, the lively satisfaction with which the conference receives the declarations which have just been made to it. The plenipotentiaries see, in the principle therein established of an appeal to the minister of foreign affairs, at once a proof of the sentiments of justice which animate His Sheriffian Majesty with regard to his Israelitish subjects, and an augury of the speedy accomplishment of the desires expressed by the conference.
The conference adjourns until Monday, the 28th of June.
The sitting ends at three o’clock.
